messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis
Details: 
The failing test `testEqualsAfterSerializationOfDerivedClass` creates an instance of a subclass `DerivedMultiKey`, serializes it, then deserializes it and checks the hash code consistency. The test fails because the hash code of the deserialized object does not match the original.

Looking at the `MultiKey` class:
- It has a transient `hashCode` field that is calculated based on the `keys`.
- It has a private `readResolve` method which recalculates the hashCode during deserialization and returns `this`.

This private `readResolve` in `MultiKey` performs a hash code recalculation after deserialization, which works fine when `MultiKey` itself is serialized and deserialized. However, the issue arises in the case of subclassing `MultiKey` (such as `DerivedMultiKey`), because Java serialization does not allow the private `readResolve` method of the superclass to be called for the subclass during deserialization. The private `readResolve` in `MultiKey` is thus effectively ignored for subclasses, leaving the transient `hashCode` field uninitialized and causing inequality after deserialization.

The current bug report explicitly describes this problem: that the `readResolve` in `MultiKey` must be protected instead of private, so that subclasses also pick up the hash code recalculation upon deserialization. Alternatively, the class `MultiKey` must be declared final to prevent subclassing issues.

This diagnosis explains why the test fails only for a subclass of `MultiKey` and after serialization. The root cause is the private visibility of the `readResolve` method in `MultiKey`, which prevents correct hash code recalculation on deserialized subclass instances. This leads to inconsistent hash codes between the original and deserialized objects.

Recent bug reports retrieved are unrelated and thus do not affect this diagnosis.

Hence, the fix involves changing the visibility of `MultiKey.readResolve()` from private to protected or making the class final to prevent erroneous subclassing behavior during deserialization.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
